source.title: SSE-SAM: Balancing Head and Tail Classes Gradually through Stage-Wise SAM
source.authors: Xingyu Lyu; Qian-Qian Xu; Zhi-Yong Yang; Shaojie Lyu; Qing-Ming Huang

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text contains the paper and appendices
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports held-out accuracy under different SAM-based training methods on long-tailed image datasets, using a setting and measures distinct from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-accuracy results for SAM, ImbSAM and SSE-SAM. It does not test any listed version: the datasets are long-tailed, and results do not measure the random-label memorization comparison, width scaling, convolutional versus fully connected models, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, or memorized-example removal. Hessian λratio results concern saddle escape and are not rows for V7.
record.test_reason: The study uses a sharpness–generalization rationale to develop and evaluate SSE-SAM, but tests none of V1–V8. Its accuracy comparisons evaluate training methods; its Hessian eigenvalue ratio measures saddle escape, not magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its correlation with training–test gaps. Theorem 6 supplies a curvature-based generalization bound, not a test of V7's empirical ranking claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: SAM and ImbSAM have complementary saddle-escape strengths, and SSE-SAM stages them to improve long-tailed classification. Their strongest performance claims require qualification: CIFAR-100-LT with LDAM gives SSE-SAM 50.9% overall versus ImbSAM 51.6%, and Table 2 includes other baselines above CE+SSE-SAM's 47.5%.
record.recipe_differences: Tests staged and class-specific SAM variants on long-tailed classification datasets; uses ResNet32, SGD with momentum 0.9 and 500 epochs. It does not reproduce the methods in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary with dataset, loss, class-frequency group, ρtail and transition factor γ. Increasing γ improves head-class performance while hurting medium and tail classes and reducing overall performance; performance peaks at ρtail = 0.10 in the reported ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: With CE on CIFAR-100-LT, SSE-SAM increases overall accuracy from 44.6% to 49.3% while reducing Many-class accuracy from 74.3% to 71.7%. On ImageNet-LT, overall accuracy increases from 45.1% to 47.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stage-wise class-specific SAM can improve long-tailed classification accuracy, with class-group tradeoffs that depend on dataset and training settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Theoretical update-direction analysis and Figure 4's absolute Hessian eigenvalue ratio characterize complementary saddle-escape behavior of SAM and ImbSAM across head and tail classes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Staging head- and tail-class perturbations can balance saddle escape across class-frequency groups.

record.problems: The experiments use artificially truncated long-tailed datasets and balanced test sets, so they do not directly establish the claim's same-distribution generalization setting. The paper says experiments were run three times, but the reported tables provide no uncertainty estimates. The text specifies ResNet32 and SGD with momentum 0.9; broader architecture and optimizer coverage is not reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 includes additional LDAM, LA and VS loss conditions, and Table 3 reports further CIFAR-100-LT comparisons across imbalance factors and perturbation settings; omitted to stay within the 60-row limit while retaining representative reported dataset, class-group and overall accuracy results. Figure-only accuracy dynamics and λratio analyses were not extracted as rows because they do not map to a listed version and lack tabulated exact values.

untested.parts: Matched random-label and natural-label training, memorization capacity, and held-out performance.
Width scaling beyond zero training error and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks, local connectivity, and transferred initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning conditions and recovery strategies.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Influence-based identification and removal of memorized examples versus matched random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The exclusion rests on missing claim-specific comparisons and measures, not on long-tailed data alone. SAM variants here use SGD as their base optimizer; they do not constitute an adaptive-versus-SGD test. Theorem 6's curvature bound and Figure 4's saddle-escape proxy do not establish or refute V7. All recorded numerical values and CE baselines match the supplied tables; their original states describe accuracy changes rather than effects named by V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label performance under the same recipe.
Width sweep past interpolation and the resulting test-error trajectory.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch comparisons and recipe adaptations.
Dropout addition/removal and its test-error effects.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness as a measure tracking the training-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the test-accuracy effect.
